content: Explain how recursion uses the call stack memory

Every time a recursive algorithm is invoked, the system allocates a new stack frame (or activation record) on the call stack [Slide 18]. This stack frame contains the function's local variables, parameters, and the return address so the program knows where to resume execution once the recursive call finishes [Slide 18]. 

For recursive execution to succeed, it must follow strict rules: it requires at least one base case to produce a direct result without further recursion, and the recurrence step must ensure that arguments strictly converge toward that base case [Page 73, Slide 18]. If a base case is omitted or implemented incorrectly (such as missing a `node == null` check in tree traversals), stack frames will accumulate monotonically until memory exhaustion results in a stack overflow exception [Page 73, 38:21].

citations.snippet: Activation Records: Every recursive invocation pushes a new stack frame containing local variables and return address.
citations.relevance_reason: Explains how individual stack frames are pushed during recursion.

citations.snippet: Without an explicit base case, call stack frames accumulate monotonically until a stack overflow exception halts the runtime.
citations.relevance_reason: Describes what happens to call stack memory when a base case is missing.
